n: Corianton has one more worry: it seems unfair for God to punish sinners with misery. Alma sets out to explain how justice and mercy work together.
Alma starts in Eden. After Adam and Eve were sent out to till the ground, God placed cherubim and a flaming sword east of the garden to guard the tree of life.

f.g: Heavenly beings who guard sacred places.

n: Having eaten the fruit of knowledge, Adam and Eve now knew good and evil. God kept them from the tree of life so they would not eat it and live forever in their fallen state.

f.w: the man had become as God, knowing good and evil

n: The result: humanity received time to repent—a “probationary time” to turn to God and serve Him.

f.g: A testing period in which to prove oneself.

n: Had Adam eaten from the tree of life immediately, he would have lived forever in his sins with no chance to repent, and God’s plan of salvation would have been defeated.
Instead, humans were appointed to die. Cut off from the tree of life, they would one day be cut off from the earth, and became “fallen man.”

f.w: it was appointed unto man to die

n: Adam and Eve were cut off from God physically (they would die) and spiritually (separated from His presence). They now had to follow their own will—agency in a fallen world.

f.w: cut off both temporally and spiritually

n: It wasn’t wise to rescue them from physical death right away, because mortality is a necessary part of the “great plan of happiness.”
But since the soul never dies and the Fall brought spiritual death—separation from God—it was necessary for humanity to be rescued from that spiritual death.
Because humans became carnal, sensual, and devilish by nature, this life became a preparatory state—a time to get ready to meet God.
Without the plan of redemption, every soul at death would be miserable, permanently cut off from the Lord.
Humans had no way to rescue themselves from this fallen state, which their own disobedience had brought.
Justice requires that redemption come only on the condition of repentance during this life. Otherwise, mercy would destroy justice—and if justice were destroyed, God would cease to be God.

f.w: God would cease to be God

n: So all humanity was fallen and held in the grip of justice, which demanded permanent separation from God.
The heart of the chapter: mercy required an atonement, so God Himself atones for the world’s sins. That way justice is satisfied and God can be both perfectly just and merciful.

f.w: God himself atoneth for the sins of the world

n: Repentance only means something if there is a real consequence. The punishment was made as eternal as the soul, set opposite the plan of happiness, which is also eternal.
Alma reasons step by step: no repentance without sin, no sin without law, no law without a punishment.

f.w: How could he sin if there was no law?

n: God set a punishment and a just law, and that law produces a guilty conscience in people who break it.
Example: if there were no law that murderers must die, would anyone fear the penalty for murder?
Likewise, without a law against sin, people wouldn’t fear sinning.
And without law, neither justice nor mercy would have any claim on a person—neither could act at all.

But there is a law, a punishment, and an opportunity to repent. Mercy claims those who repent; justice claims everyone else and carries out the penalty. Otherwise justice would be destroyed and God would not be God.
God remains God: mercy claims the penitent because of the atonement. The atonement brings resurrection, which brings everyone back into God’s presence to be judged by their works.

f.w: the atonement bringeth to pass the resurrection

n: Justice gets everything it is owed, and mercy claims all that is hers. So only the truly repentant are saved.
Can mercy cheat justice? Not one bit. If it could, God would no longer be God. Christ paid justice in full.
This is how God accomplishes His eternal purposes, prepared before the world began—bringing salvation to some and, by their choice, misery to others.

f.w: from the foundation of the world

n: Whoever wants to come may freely drink from the waters of life; no one is forced. At the last day, each is restored according to their deeds.

f.w: whosoever will come may come and partake of the waters of life freely

n: Someone who chose evil and never repented will receive evil, according to God’s law of restoration.
Alma tells Corianton to stop being troubled about God’s fairness. Only let your sins trouble you—in a way that leads you to repent.

f.w: only let your sins trouble you

n: Don’t deny God’s justice to excuse your sins. Let His justice, mercy, and patience fully govern your heart and humble you to the dust.
Alma restores Corianton to his calling: go preach with truth and seriousness, bring souls to repentance so mercy can claim them. A later passage shows Corianton did return to the work.

f.w: ye are called of God to preach the word
